pageName: Cats With Kidney Disease Support Group
adCopy: I am so f*cking tired of watching women with kidney cats get told that irreversible means nothing can get better. IT DOES NOT MEAN THAT. AND NOBODY IN THAT COMMENT SECTION HAS EVER BEEN MADE TO SAY WHICH PART THEY MEAN. I read one this morning. A woman asking if anything had ever brought a creatinine down, and eleven people telling her, kindly, to focus on comfort now. Every one of them meant well. Every one of them was repeating a word nobody had ever defined for them either. I know because I did what they told her to do. For eighteen months. I know because I bought every food. Both binders. Porus One. A tub of something from an American group that came in a padded envelope with no English on it, and I am 61 years old and I still bought it. I know because I learned to put a needle under my cat's skin off a video, at sixty, with my hands shaking so badly I had to put the bag down and start again. $2,900. Four vets. An internal medicine specialist. An ultrasound. And Judith went 2.8. 3.0. 3.2. 3.4. The cat before her was a ginger tom called Ivan. He died at nine. Kidney failure. He weighed 5.9 pounds and I could close one hand right around his back leg. I sat on the kitchen floor with him for an hour afterwards and could not make myself phone anybody. And I did the exact same things for Judith that I did for him. Because I believed the same thing you are believing right now. Nothing in your cabinet was ever built to move her creatinine. Not the k/d. Not Epakitin. Not Pronefra. Not the $68 bag they put in your hands the day they said the word. None of it is aimed at what is taking her kidneys. Every single thing on that list is cleaning up after it. There is something being built inside her kidneys right now. Not taken away. Built. It wraps around the parts that still work and squeezes them a bit harder every month. You cannot see it. She cannot tell you. And it decides which of these two you get. Two more years. Her on the windowsill, eating, herself, annoyed with you. Or having her put down in a few months. On a table, in a back room, with somebody telling you kindly that sometimes this just happens. It is that. It is literally that. Read this entire post. Every word. I don't care if you're busy and I don't care that it's long. Because the answer is in here and it is NOT another thing to manage her numbers with. 🙏 I'm Marion. I'm 61. I taught high school biology in Erie for twenty-six years, and my cat is a brown tabby called Judith who has been sitting on my grading since 2016. She was diagnosed stage 3 the October before last. Creatinine 2.8. Let me tell you what the eighteen months after that actually looked like, because I suspect a lot of it is yours. Judith drinks constantly. Out of the tap. Off the shower floor. Out of my glass if I leave it on the side for ten minutes. I change a soaked litter box twice a day now and I buy the heavy bags. The food is its own job, and it is the job that never ends. She had four flavors she liked in the spring. She has one now. And every time one goes, it goes for good. She sniffs it, does that little lip lick, walks away, and that is that flavor finished forever. They never come back. There are eleven cans in my cabinet and two of them are any use. I have warmed it. Watered it. Raised the bowl on a paperback. Put it on a saucer instead of a dish because somebody said the whiskers matter. I have sat on my own kitchen floor at nine thirty at night, holding food out on my finger. She will sometimes take it off a finger. She will not take it off a plate. Some nights she licks the juice off and leaves everything underneath. I learned to give fluids off a video at sixty years old. My hands shook so badly the first time I had to put the bag down and start again. And I weigh her. Sundays, on the kitchen scales, in a shoebox, because that is the only way she stays still. I have a note on my phone with eighteen months of her weights in it and I open it far more often than is good for me. 😔 9.8. 9.5. 9.1. 8.8. 8.6. That note is the real diary of this disease. Not the panels. Here is the list, with what each thing actually did, because I kept a record like the teacher I am. Hill's k/d. $68 a bag. Lowers the phosphorus and protein load. She ate it for five weeks and then would not touch it again. Did exactly what it said. Was never going to move a number. Royal Canin renal. Same job. She lasted about a month. Same verdict. Epakitin, then Pronefra when her phosphorus crept anyway. Both worked. Her phosphorus has been fine for a year. And her creatinine climbed the entire time they were working. Porus One. Eight weeks. I could not point to one thing that changed. Out. Fluids twice a week. She is visibly better for about a day. Then it wears off and you do it again on Thursday. A top-up. Not a treatment. Everybody knows that and nobody says it. Taurine, because it is all over the ads right now. I asked my vet directly. She said taurine is sold so people can make their own cat food safely, and a cat on wet food is not short of it. Out. $34. A tub of something from an American group that arrived in a padded envelope with no English on the label. I am 61 years old and I bought it anyway. That is how far gone I was. 😔 2.8 at diagnosis. 3.0 the next spring. 3.2 in the fall. 3.4 in March. Look at that list properly. Every single thing on it is holding a line. Not one of them is trying to take ground. And when I asked why there was nothing that took ground, I got one word back. Every time. From every one of them. Irreversible. And here is the thing I need to say about those four vets, because I think it matters more than anything else in this post. Not one of them was unkind to me. Not one of them lied. Not one of them was wrong. That is what makes this so hard to see. Nobody is the villain. Everybody is gentle with you. And every single conversation, in the nicest possible way, is managing your expectations downward, until one day you notice you have stopped asking questions and started nodding. My sister said, gently, she has had a good run. The group said try not to get your hopes up. And I nodded at all of it. Twenty-six years of teaching sixteen year olds to define their terms. And I sat in those rooms nodding at a word I could not have explained if you had asked me to. That is the bit I am still angry about. Not at them. At me. So in March I did the thing I should have done in the first week. I went back in and I made her define it. I said: irreversible, which part? And she stopped. And I want to be fair to her, she did not get defensive, she thought about it. Then she said, honestly, probably not, when I asked her whether the filters Judith still has were working as well as they possibly could be. I said, why not? And she told me about scarring. Here is what she explained, and I have read enough since to be able to say it back properly. Her kidneys are made of tiny filters. Hundreds of thousands of them. They're called nephrons, and they are the part that actually cleans the blood. When one gets damaged, it heals over with scar. Same as your skin does. The name for that scar in a kidney is fibrosis. Normally the scarring stops once the healing is done. With this disease the damage never stops. So the scarring never stops either. Month after month, year after year. And here is the part that made me put my pen down. That scar does not fill in the gaps where filters have already died. It grows around the filters that are still alive, and it squeezes them until they can barely work. I taught diffusion across a membrane for a quarter of a century. I know exactly what happens to a filter when you wrap it in something and tighten. It does not die. It just stops being able to do very much. Those filters are not dead. They are being strangled. Tonight, while she is asleep on the good chair. You cannot see it happening. She cannot tell you. And her blood test will not show it until so many filters have been squeezed shut that she has nothing left to cover with. That is the day it all falls apart at once, and it is why people say she was fine and then suddenly she wasn't. So there it was. Irreversible, which part? The filters she has already lost. Those are gone. She cannot grow new ones. That is true, it was always true, and anybody who tells you different is lying to you. The ones she still has, being squeezed by scar, are a completely different problem. One of those is finished. The other one is happening right now. And every single thing on my list was aimed at the first one. Then the obvious question, which took me another two weeks to ask. If the damage is what keeps the scarring switched on, what switches it off? The swelling. The swelling is what keeps telling the kidney to lay more down. Bring the swelling down and the building slows. And when the building slows, the squeeze eases, and filters that were being strangled get to work again. They were never dead. They were just being held. I did the cheap version first, because of course I did. Nineteen dollars of fish oil off Amazon. Six weeks. Salmon flavored, which I should have thought harder about at the time. Nothing moved. So I went and found out why, and there are two things I had genuinely never understood in eighteen months of buying supplements. Omega-3 is not one thing. There are two that matter and they do different jobs, and in feline kidney disease DHA is the one tied to less inflammation. Not the other one. Every bottle I had bought just said omega-3 on the front and never once said which way it leaned. And the source changes how much actually arrives. It has been measured in cats, side by side. Cats given DHA from algae ended up with more of it in their blood than cats given DHA from fish oil. Same nutrient. Different vehicle. Different amount getting where it is going. The one I use is Catopia Marine Algae Oil. Algae oil first, with organic hemp seed oil and organic flaxseed oil behind it. I looked at where it comes from, because old habits. One site, a peninsula in Iceland, cold North Atlantic on three sides and geothermal power out of the ground underneath it. The cold is the point. In cold water the algae has to build more of the fat that keeps its own cell membranes working, and that fat is DHA. One traceable source, rather than oils from anywhere blended together and called omega-3. And it pours onto her food. No pill. No needle. Judith stopped letting me near her with a tablet in 2024 and I have never got that back. Anything that has to be given to her does not happen in this house any more. Four seconds. She has no idea it is happening. Week two, nothing. I want to say that, because I nearly stopped. Week four, she ate a whole bowl in one go. First time since the summer. I stood in the kitchen and watched her do it like an idiot. Week seven, she came up onto the bed, which she had stopped doing in February. Week eleven, the panel. Judith's March panel and her July panel, side by side. Creatinine 3.4, then 2.5. BUN 52, then 38. Phosphorus 5.9, then 4.6. And she has put on nine ounces, which at her size is not nothing. ❤️ Her vet wrote "IRIS stage 2" at the top of the July one. She had been stage 3 since the October before last. I am not going to sit here and tell you her kidneys are fixed. They are not. The filters she already lost are lost. Her scan looks exactly as bad as it did. That was true when the first vet said it and it is true now. But something moved. After eighteen months of watching a number go one way, something moved the other way, and I got there by taking one word apart. If your vet has told you irreversible, she is not wrong. Ask her which part. 🙏 https://catopia.shop/products/catopia-marine-algae-oil P.S. I never asked a question like that in eighteen months of appointments, and I made a living asking sixteen year olds to define their terms. I have thought about that a lot. I think when you are frightened you stop behaving like yourself, and everybody in the room is too kind to point it out.

Those are gone. She cannot grow new ones. That is true, it was always true, and anybody who tells you different is lying to you. The ones she still has, being squeezed by scar, are a completely different problem. One of those is finished. The other one is happening right now. And every single thing on my list was aimed at the first one. Then the obvious question, which took me another two weeks to ask. If the damage is what keeps the scarring switched on, what switches it off? The swelling. The swelling is what keeps telling the kidney to lay more down. Bring the swelling down and the building slows. And when the building slows, the squeeze eases, and filters that were being strangled get to work again. They were never dead. They were just being held. I did the cheap version first, because of course I did. Nineteen dollars of fish oil off Amazon. Six weeks. Salmon flavored, which I should have thought harder about at the time. Nothing moved. So I went and found out why, and there are two things I had genuinely never understood in eighteen months of buying supplements. Omega-3 is not one thing. There are two that matter and they do different jobs, and in feline kidney disease DHA is the one tied to less inflammation. Not the other one. Every bottle I had bought just said omega-3 on the front and never once said which way it leaned. And the source changes how much actually arrives. It has been measured in cats, side by side. Cats given DHA from algae ended up with more of it in their blood than cats given DHA from fish oil. Same nutrient. Different vehicle. Different amount getting where it is going. The one I use is Catopia Marine Algae Oil. Algae oil first, with organic hemp seed oil and organic flaxseed oil behind it. I looked at where it comes from, because old habits. One site, a peninsula in Iceland, cold North Atlantic on three sides and geothermal power out of the ground underneath it. The cold is the point. In cold water the algae has to build more of the fat that keeps its own cell membranes working, and that fat is DHA. One traceable source, rather than oils from anywhere blended together and called omega-3. And it pours onto her food. No pill. No needle. Judith stopped letting me near her with a tablet in 2024 and I have never got that back. Anything that has to be given to her does not happen in this house any more. Four seconds. She has no idea it is happening. Week two, nothing. I want to say that, because I nearly stopped. Week four, she ate a whole bowl in one go. First time since the summer. I stood in the kitchen and watched her do it like an idiot. Week seven, she came up onto the bed, which she had stopped doing in February. Week eleven, the panel. Judith's March panel and her July panel, side by side. Creatinine 3.4, then 2.5. BUN 52, then 38. Phosphorus 5.9, then 4.6. And she has put on nine ounces, which at her size is not nothing. ❤️ Her vet wrote "IRIS stage 2" at the top of the July one. She had been stage 3 since the October before last. I am not going to sit here and tell you her kidneys are fixed. They are not. The filters she already lost are lost. Her scan looks exactly as bad as it did. That was true when the first vet said it and it is true now. But something moved. After eighteen months of watching a number go one way, something moved the other way, and I got there by taking one word apart. If your vet has told you irreversible, she is not wrong. Ask her which part. 🙏 https://catopia.shop/products/catopia-marine-algae-oil P.S. I never asked a question like that in eighteen months of appointments, and I made a living asking sixteen year olds to define their terms. I have thought about that a lot. I think when you are frightened you stop behaving like yourself, and everybody in the room is too kind to point it out.

adCopy: He reached for his inhaler twice that week, and both times he'd just walked past the hall closet. I didn't think anything of it the first time. Miles has had asthma since he was a kid, it's just part of who he is, like some people carry sunglasses, he carries an inhaler. Second time, same week, same spot, I noticed it but still didn't say anything. We've got a cat, Moose, he's 4, and his litter box lives in that hall closet, always has, small apartment, not a lot of options. I scoop every day, keep the door mostly shut, never thought twice about it. We've been in this place about 2 years, one bedroom, and that closet's really the only spot for the box unless we want it sitting in the kitchen. Third time was on a Sunday. Miles walked past that closet carrying laundry, and about 10 seconds later he was standing in the kitchen with his inhaler out, coughing into his elbow. I asked if he was ok and he said yeah, just a rough week for his lungs, happens sometimes. I believed him, because why wouldn't I, he'd say the same thing every few months, some weeks are just worse than others. But I started noticing it more after that Sunday. Not every day, but enough days that I started keeping a weird little mental note without meaning to. Home days, near that hallway a lot, he'd use it. Days we were both out, or he worked from the office, nothing. He started doing this thing without even noticing, grabbing his inhaler off the counter before he'd walk down that hallway, like his hand knew something before his head did. I brought it up once, kind of careful, asked if he thought it was connected to anything in the apartment. He laughed and said no, it's just asthma, it does its own thing, you can't always find a reason. I let it go. Told myself I was overthinking a hallway. Then one night he had a coughing fit bad enough that I got out of bed and sat with him on the edge of the tub until it passed. His breathing had that thin, whistly sound to it, the one that always means it's worse than he's letting on. I didn't say much, I just sat there rubbing his back until it evened out. That scared me more than I want to admit. Not because it was some emergency, it wasn't, he was fine within a few minutes. It scared me because I realized I'd been watching this happen in slow motion for months and calling it normal. I know how that sounds, blaming a cat box for somebody's asthma. I thought the same thing at first. I mentioned it to my friend Priya, she's a nurse, mostly just venting, not expecting an actual answer. And she stopped me and asked exactly where his inhaler use was worse. I said the hallway, by the closet, and she got quiet for a second. She said asthma lungs don't work like a normal nose. A normal nose needs something to build up pretty strong before it even registers, but an airway that's already sensitive can react to way less than that, sometimes so little a person standing right next to him wouldn't smell a thing. She said it's not really about how much is in the room, it's about how sensitive the thing breathing it is, some people could stand in there all day and feel nothing. She said cat urine breaks down into ammonia gas, and ammonia's a known airway irritant, it doesn't need to be strong enough for me to notice it for it to be strong enough to bother him. Which explained something that had been bugging me the whole time, why I never smelled anything different in that hallway, not once, not even on his worst weeks. I wasn't wrong for not smelling it. I was just never going to be the one who caught it, because his lungs were reacting to something my nose was never built to flag in the first place. That part actually made me a little sick to think about, that his body had basically been warning us for months and we kept calling it a rough week. She mentioned something she'd started using at her own place, some little plug in thing by the litter box, said it wasn't a filter, said it worked on the gas itself instead of just the smell. Called it ScentGuard. I know, another plug in thing, I've seen plenty of those. But she wasn't trying to sell me anything, she was just telling me what she used, so I looked into it. From what she told me, it runs all the time, breaking the gas apart before it can build up in a closed space like that closet, so it's working whether or not anyone's nose, mine or his, ever picks up on anything. That part is what got me, honestly, it wasn't about making the hallway smell better, it was about there being less of it there to begin with. I ordered one that week, $39.99, plugged it in right next to Moose's box. Didn't say much to Miles about it, just wanted to see what happened first. 2 weeks in, I started keeping that same mental note again, except this time on purpose. Home days. Near the hallway. Nothing. He hasn't reached for it walking past that closet once since, not that I've seen anyway. He still keeps one in his bag, he probably always will, that's just part of having asthma. But the specific thing, the hallway thing, the pattern I'd been quietly tracking for months without telling him, it just stopped showing up. A few weeks after that he had his regular checkup with his pulmonologist and mentioned, almost as a side note, that he hadn't needed a rescue puff at home in a while. She didn't say anything about a plug in device, obviously, she just noted it down as an improvement and moved on to the next thing. I told him eventually, showed him the little notes I'd kept on my phone without really meaning to. He got kind of quiet looking at it. Said he never even put it together himself, he just figured some weeks were worse, the way they'd always been. Moose still uses the same box, same spot, nothing about our actual routine changed. I don't think about that hallway anymore, honestly. I used to walk past it and half brace, waiting to hear him cough from another room. I don't do that anymore either. It's just a closet now, with a cat box in it, the way it was always supposed to be.

adCopy: I threw away 23 cans of the most expensive cat food I’d ever bought last October. At 2:11 that morning, I climbed into the trash and pulled every one back out. Not because they were expired. Not because Oliver refused to eat them. Because of one question my daughter asked me at dinner that I couldn’t answer: “How much of the taurine written on that label is Oliver actually getting?” I stared at her. Then I looked beneath the kitchen table, where Oliver had been sleeping since before dinner. And suddenly, every little change I’d spent the past year explaining away felt connected. My name is Susan. I’m 61 years old, and Oliver is my 11-year-old cat. He has been part of our family for so long that I can measure entire chapters of my life by the places he used to wait for me. At our first house, it was the bedroom window. After we moved, it became the top step. And for the past six years, it has been the bathroom counter. Every morning, Oliver would follow me into the bathroom, jump beside the sink and shove his head beneath the faucet before I finished brushing my teeth. He never drank from it properly. He would let the water run across his forehead, shake it all over the mirror and walk through the puddle with his paws. I complained about those wet paw prints almost every morning. Then one day, they disappeared. I didn’t notice immediately. That’s the cruel thing about a cat slowing down. It rarely happens all at once. There’s no single morning when they wake up and announce that something has changed. It happens one missing habit at a time. First, Oliver stopped jumping onto the bathroom counter. Then he stopped waiting outside our bedroom. Then he started pausing halfway up the stairs. He still ate. He still used his litter box. He still purred when I touched him. So every individual change came with an innocent explanation. “He’s getting older.” “He’s comfortable.” “Cats sleep more as they age.” “He probably doesn’t care about the faucet anymore.” That last one came from my husband. I wanted to believe him. But I knew Oliver. That faucet wasn’t simply somewhere he drank. It was part of who he was. This was the cat who once pushed an entire glass of water off my nightstand because I wouldn’t turn the bathroom faucet on quickly enough. He hadn’t suddenly stopped caring. He had stopped making the trip. Soon, other pieces of him started disappearing too. He stopped following me into the laundry room. He stopped appearing every time I opened the refrigerator. He stopped carrying his fabric mouse through the hallway at night. He stopped meeting our daughter at the door when she visited. He would lie beneath the kitchen table and watch everything happening around him. Awake. Quiet. Present, but somehow no longer participating. I bought softer food. Then senior food. Then grain-free food. Then refrigerated food that cost more than some of our own meals. Every new box made me feel better for a few days because buying something felt like doing something. I would carefully transition him, watch his bowl and convince myself that he seemed slightly different. But after a week, Oliver would be back beneath the kitchen table. Last October, I opened the pantry and saw 23 cans left from the latest food I had tried. Premium ingredients. Complete and balanced. Taurine added. Everything I thought I was supposed to look for was printed directly on the label. And Oliver still wasn’t acting like Oliver. Something in me snapped. I took every can from the pantry, dropped them into the kitchen trash and told my husband I was finished wasting money. That evening, our daughter came for dinner. She found Oliver beneath the table and sat on the floor beside him. She had lived with us when Oliver’s faucet obsession began, so she remembered the wet bathroom counter too. After a few minutes, she looked at me and asked when he had stopped jumping. I told her it had been months. She picked up one of the empty cans beside the sink and started reading it. Then she asked: “Mom, cats can’t make taurine themselves, right?” I said that was why I bought food with taurine in it. She looked at the label again. Then she asked the question that kept me awake: “But how much of what goes into this food survives everything that happens before it reaches Oliver?” I didn’t know. At 2:11 that morning, I went downstairs, opened the trash and pulled every can back out. I arranged them across the kitchen floor and read every label. Some mentioned taurine in the ingredient list. Some didn’t show an actual amount. Some used nearly identical language even though the foods looked, smelled and cost completely different. I kept searching for the number that would tell me how much taurine Oliver had actually consumed. I couldn’t find it. So I opened my laptop. That was the beginning of a six-hour rabbit hole that changed how I looked at every bowl of cat food I had ever served. The first thing I learned was something I should have understood years ago: Cats are different. Their bodies cannot manufacture enough taurine to cover what they use. They must obtain it through their diet, consistently, throughout their entire lives. Not occasionally. Not only when they’re young. Every day. Because taurine isn’t sitting in one place doing one job. A cat’s heart uses taurine to support the movement of calcium inside its muscle cells—the cellular process behind each steady contraction. Their retinas maintain extremely high concentrations of taurine to support the cells responsible for vision. Their muscles and nerves depend on it for normal cellular signaling and fluid balance. Their liver attaches taurine to bile acids so the body can digest fat. Then part of that taurine leaves through digestion. Which means a cat isn’t simply receiving taurine. They are constantly spending it. Every heartbeat. Every movement. Every meal. Every day. Then I discovered the part that bothered me. The amount of taurine used when food is formulated isn’t automatically the same as the amount a particular cat ultimately consumes, absorbs, retains and uses. Food is heated, processed, stored and exposed to moisture before it reaches the bowl. Oliver doesn’t finish every meal. Some days he eats around the edges and leaves the middle. Sometimes we change flavors. Sometimes his digestion is different. His body continually uses taurine to make bile, and some of it can leave through the digestive tract instead of being recycled. I even found research explaining why canned cat food has historically required substantially more added taurine than dry food to maintain the same taurine status inside the cat. Not because cats eating wet food suddenly require a different nutrient. Because processing, digestion, gut activity and taurine loss can change how much remains available to the body. That was the moment everything clicked. I started calling it “the Taurine Tax.” The Taurine Tax is the invisible distance between the taurine that exists on paper and the taurine a cat actually consumes, retains and uses. The label describes what was formulated into the food. It cannot show me what happened during every step before that food reached Oliver. It cannot show me how much he left in the bowl. It cannot show me how much his body absorbed. It cannot show me how much was lost through digestion. And it cannot show me whether the tissues depending on taurine every day were receiving consistent support. Older cats don’t receive a discount on that tax. Their hearts still beat. Their retinas still work. Their nerves still fire. Their bodies still digest fat. They still depend on taurine for the same systems they have relied on their entire lives. That’s when the 23 cans scattered across my kitchen stopped looking like 23 different solutions. They were different versions of the same unanswered question. I want to make something clear. I didn’t decide cat food was bad. I didn’t stop feeding Oliver. I realized that repeatedly changing his entire diet might never answer the one question keeping me awake: Was Oliver consistently getting the taurine support his body depended on every day? I started looking for a way to add taurine after the manufacturing, heating and storage had already happened. Something simple. Something measured. Something I could mix directly into food Oliver was already willing to eat. No giant ingredient blend. No treats filled with flavors and fillers. No pills I would have to force down his throat. Just taurine. That is when I found SuperTaurine. It was made specifically for cats. It contained pure taurine without a complicated list of unrelated ingredients. It was third-party tested. And instead of hoping enough taurine had survived every step before Oliver’s food reached our house, I could add a measured serving directly to the finished food. At the final step. Right before he ate it. I ordered it that morning. When the tub arrived, I measured the serving and mixed it into a small amount of wet food Oliver reliably finished. He didn’t smell it and walk away. He didn’t stare at me like I had destroyed his breakfast. He ate normally. Nothing dramatic happened that first day. He didn’t suddenly race through the house. He didn’t leap onto the counter. And honestly, I’m glad he didn’t. After watching Oliver change gradually, an overnight miracle would have felt ridiculous. So I stopped waiting for fireworks. I started watching for Oliver. On day 13, I came out of the bedroom and found him sitting in the doorway. He hadn’t waited there in months. He didn’t follow me downstairs. He simply sat there watching me. But it was the first old habit that had returned. A week later, I opened the refrigerator and felt something brush against my ankle. Oliver. Standing exactly where he used to stand, waiting to see what I was taking out. My husband noticed him becoming more present during the evenings. Our daughter visited and said his eyes looked more alert. I didn’t tell either of them what I wanted to hear. I kept the routine the same and continued watching. Then, on day 36, I was brushing my teeth when I heard his paws land on the bathroom counter. I froze. Oliver walked toward the sink and looked at the faucet. I turned it on. He pushed his head directly beneath the water. Then he shook it across the mirror, stepped through the puddle and walked away. Four wet paw prints remained on the counter. I stood there staring at them until my husband asked what was wrong. I started crying. Not because Oliver had performed some spectacular trick. Because he had done something annoying. Something ordinary. Something so completely Oliver that I hadn’t understood how badly I missed it until it happened again. That is the part of a cat slowing down that nobody prepares you for. You don’t only miss their energy. You miss the inconvenience. The toy dropped outside your bedroom. The cat standing in front of the refrigerator. The paws on the counter you just cleaned. The sound of them following you into a room where they have absolutely no reason to be. Those little behaviors are their identity. Sometimes you don’t understand what they meant until they disappear. Oliver has now been part of this routine for 90 days. He is still 11. I’m not pretending taurine turned him into a kitten. But he is no longer spending every evening beneath the kitchen table. He follows me upstairs again. He waits near the refrigerator. He sits outside the bedroom. And most mornings, I wipe wet paw prints from the bathroom counter.
